01: President Lincoln signs the Pacific Railway Act, authorizing the Union Pacific and Central Pacific to build a railroad from the Missouri River at Council Bluffs, Iowa, to Sacramento, California.
The radiotelegraph convention signed in 1906 takes effect, making SOS - three dots, three dashes, three dots - the distress signal for ships at sea. Germany has used it since 1905.
At 2:30 p.m., before a Dodgers-Phillies game, New York station WNBT shows a clock face marked 'Bulova Watch Time' for one minute: the first paid television advertisement in the United States.
02: President Lincoln signs the Morrill Act. Each state gets 30,000 acres of public land per member of Congress to fund colleges teaching agriculture and the mechanic arts: the land-grant colleges.
Amelia Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan take off from Lae, New Guinea, in a Lockheed Electra for Howland Island, 2,556 miles away. They never arrive. She is declared dead in 1939.
03: Karl Benz takes his three-wheeled motor car on a trip around Mannheim, reported in the local paper: the first public outing of the Patent-Motorwagen. Its engine makes about one horsepower.
On Stoke Bank, south of Grantham, England, driver Joseph Duddington takes Nigel Gresley's locomotive Mallard to 126 mph. No steam locomotive has officially gone faster.
04: Charles Carroll of Carrollton, almost 91 and the last living signer of the Declaration of Independence, lays the first stone of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad. It is his last public act.
President Grant dedicates the Eads Bridge at St. Louis, seven years in the building. James Eads' 520-foot center arch is the longest rigid span yet built, and it pioneers the use of steel.
Mars Pathfinder lands on airbags in Ares Vallis, carrying the 23-pound rover Sojourner: the first rover to operate beyond the Earth and Moon. Its last data arrives on September 27.
05: Germany opens Operation Citadel against the Soviet lines around Kursk: 2,928 German tanks against 5,128 Soviet. The fighting lasts until August 23: the deadliest armored battle in history.
Jeff Bezos incorporates Cadabra, Inc., in Washington state, working from the garage of his house in Bellevue. As Amazon it opens for business as an online bookseller on July 16, 1995.
06: The British airship R34 reaches Mineola, Long Island, 108 hours out of East Fortune, Scotland, with only a few gallons of fuel left: the first east-to-west crossing of the Atlantic by air.
07: The Chillicothe Baking Company of Chillicothe, Missouri, sells the first sliced bread, cut on Otto Rohwedder's machine. Its ads call it the greatest forward step in baking since bread was wrapped.
On her maiden voyage the liner United States crosses the Atlantic in 3 days, 10 hours, 40 minutes at 35.59 knots, beating by more than 10 hours the record Queen Mary had held for 14 years.
08: Atlantis lifts off at 11:29 a.m. Eastern with a crew of four on STS-135, the 135th and final mission of the Space Shuttle program. She lands on July 21.
09: About 7:20 a.m. two Nashville, Chattanooga and St. Louis passenger trains collide at Dutchman's Curve in Nashville. 101 die and at least 171 are hurt: the worst rail accident in U.S. history.
10: Furnace Creek in Death Valley, California, records 134 degrees Fahrenheit: still the highest temperature on record anywhere in the world, though some meteorologists doubt the reading.
The date Britain counts as the start of the Battle of Britain, which runs to October 31: the first major military campaign fought entirely by air forces. In July the Luftwaffe hits coastal convoys.
Telstar 1, built by Bell Labs for AT&T, is launched from Cape Canaveral: a 170-pound sphere 35 inches across. On July 23 it relays the first live television signal across the Atlantic.
11: Skylab, launched in 1973 and home to three crews, falls to Earth, scattering debris across the Indian Ocean and Western Australia. The Shire of Esperance fines NASA A$400 for littering.
President Biden unveils the first image from the James Webb Space Telescope: the galaxy cluster SMACS 0723 as it was 4.6 billion years ago, seen with a 6.5-meter mirror of 18 gold-coated segments.
12: Five days of extreme heat begin in Chicago. Midway Airport reaches 106 degrees on July 13, and 739 heat-related deaths are counted in the city.
13: Live Aid: concerts at Wembley Stadium in London and JFK Stadium in Philadelphia are linked by satellite for 16 hours. An estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 nations watch on television.
14: Mariner 4 flies past Mars, 6,118 miles up, and stores 21 pictures on its tape recorder: the first images of another planet returned from deep space. Each takes about six hours to send home.
15: Nintendo releases the Family Computer in Japan for 14,800 yen, with Donkey Kong, Donkey Kong Jr. and Popeye. Designed by Masayuki Uemura, it reaches America two years later as the NES.
16: The world's first parking meter is installed in Oklahoma City. Newspaper publisher Carl Magee asked for the design; two Oklahoma State engineering professors, Thuesen and Hale, worked it out.
At 5:29 a.m. in the Jornada del Muerto desert of New Mexico, the 'gadget' explodes on a 100-foot steel tower with the force of 25 kilotons of TNT. Trinity is the first detonation of a nuclear weapon.
17: At 10:18 p.m. munitions being loaded on the cargo ship E. A. Bryan explode at Port Chicago, California. 320 die, 202 of them African-American. Fifty men are later convicted of mutiny.
At 7:05 p.m. two walkways in the Hyatt Regency in Kansas City, Missouri, fall onto a tea dance in the lobby. 114 die and 216 are hurt. A change to the hanger rods had doubled the load on the beams.
18: Gordon Moore and Robert Noyce, backed by Arthur Rock, found NM Electronics in Mountain View, California. It becomes Intel, for Integrated Electronics. Its first product is a 64-bit memory chip.
19: Prince Albert attends the float-out at Bristol of Brunel's Great Britain, 322 feet long, the largest vessel yet built and the first large ocean-going ship with an iron hull and a screw propeller.
20: The lunar module Eagle lands in the Sea of Tranquility. Hours later Neil Armstrong steps onto the Moon: 'one small step for [a] man, one giant leap for mankind.' Some 600 million people watch.
Viking 1 lands in Chryse Planitia: the first successful Mars lander. Planned for July 4, the landing waited while a smoother site was found. The lander works until November 1982.
21: Vostok Station, 11,444 feet up on the Antarctic ice, records minus 128.6 degrees Fahrenheit: the lowest natural temperature ever reliably measured on Earth.
22: Wiley Post returns to Floyd Bennett Field, New York, after 7 days, 18 hours, 49 minutes: the first to fly around the world alone, with an autopilot in place of a navigator. 50,000 people greet him.
Mariner 1, bound for Venus, veers off course and is destroyed 293 seconds after launch. A missing overline in the guidance equations costs $18.5 million: 'the most expensive hyphen in history.'
23: Chicago dentist Ernest Pfennig becomes the first owner of a Ford: a two-cylinder, 8-horsepower Model A, base price $750. Ford Motor Company has $223.65 left in the bank.
Commodore introduces the Amiga at Lincoln Center in New York, with Andy Warhol and Debbie Harry on hand: a 68000 processor, 256 KB of memory, 4,096 colors and preemptive multitasking.
24: The steamer Eastland, with 2,500 aboard for a Western Electric company picnic, rolls over at her dock in the Chicago River. 844 die: the largest loss of life from a shipwreck on the Great Lakes.
Apollo 11 splashes down in the Pacific after 8 days, 3 hours and 18 minutes, and the carrier USS Hornet picks up the crew. They bring home 47.5 pounds of the Moon.
25: About 11:10 p.m., in thick fog off Nantucket, the Swedish liner Stockholm hits the Italian liner Andrea Doria. 51 die; 1,660 of the 1,706 aboard Andrea Doria are saved before she sinks at 10:09 a.m.
26: NASA launches Syncom 2, built by Hughes Aircraft: the world's first geosynchronous communications satellite. In August it carries a call between President Kennedy and Nigeria's prime minister.
27: The steamship Great Eastern reaches Heart's Content, Newfoundland, in thick fog, and the Atlantic cable goes into service. It sends 8 words a minute. The 1858 cable had lasted three weeks.
John Cunningham takes the de Havilland Comet up from Hatfield, England, on its first flight: the world's first commercial jet airliner, with four Ghost turbojets in its wing roots.
28: At 9:40 a.m., in thick fog, an Army B-25 bomber hits the Empire State Building between the 78th and 80th floors. 14 die. Elevator operator Betty Lou Oliver survives a 75-story fall.
29: President Eisenhower signs the National Aeronautics and Space Act, close on the heels of Sputnik. It creates NASA, which takes over the work of the old NACA on October 1.
30: Fifteen minutes after midnight the submarine I-58 torpedoes the cruiser Indianapolis, which has just delivered atomic bomb parts to Tinian. She sinks in 12 minutes. Of 1,195 men, 316 survive.
At 9:05 a.m. the Volkswagen plant at Puebla, Mexico, builds the last original Beetle. 21,529,464 were made in all.
31: On Apollo 15, David Scott and Jim Irwin take the first drive on the Moon. The Boeing-built Lunar Roving Vehicle weighs 460 pounds and runs on two silver-zinc batteries. It covers 17.25 miles.
Up to 7.5 inches of rain in an hour sends a flood down Colorado's Big Thompson Canyon, cresting at 30 feet. At least 144 die, the day before the 100th anniversary of Colorado statehood.
